The AJCC 8th edition removed microscopic extrathyroidal extension (mETE) from T staging, and the 2025 ATA guidelines maintained this approach. However, prior studies remain heterogeneous and have largely relied on staging-derived surrogate endpoints rather than structural disease outcomes. We evaluated whether endpoint selection may explain these differing conclusions in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC).

We studied 3,278 PTC patients with pathologist-verified extrathyroidal extension subtyping. The primary endpoint was a 3-tier composite recurrence-risk proxy analyzed using ordinal logistic regression. Structural recurrence, defined by imaging-confirmed pathologic lymphadenopathy or reoperation (504 events), was assessed using propensity score matching (711 pairs), size-stratified models, and interaction testing. CT timing relative to index surgery was examined to assess potential peri-operative ascertainment bias. A parallel systematic review screened 819 studies and included 80.

mETE showed differing associations depending on endpoint. For the composite proxy, mETE was associated with lower odds of a higher risk category (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.51–0.72). In contrast, in the propensity-matched cohort, mETE was associated with higher structural disease (14.5% vs. 10.6%; OR 1.43, p = 0.030). A significant mETE × nodal status interaction (OR 0.36, p = 0.006) suggested that this association was concentrated in node-negative patients. AJCC 8th edition downstaged 71.5% of mETE patients. Among CT-detected pathologic lymphadenopathy events in 331 patients with ≥1 flagged examination, 508 events (40.8%) were preoperative and 73 (5.9%) were perioperative (≤30 days post-surgery), together comprising 46.7% of events likely reflecting staging workup; 174 (14.0%) occurred at 31–365 days; and 490 (39.4%) beyond one year, supporting that the structural endpoint predominantly reflected postoperative disease.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) accounts for approximately 85% of thyroid cancers, with an estimated 44,020 new cases diagnosed in the United States in 2024.1 Despite excellent long-term survival, management remains contentious regarding the pathologic features that should drive treatment intensity.2,3 Extrathyroidal extension (ETE)—tumor invasion beyond the thyroid capsule—exists along a biological continuum from microscopic perithyroidal soft tissue involvement to gross invasion of adjacent structures.

The AJCC 7th edition classified any ETE, including microscopic extension, as T3.4 The AJCC 8th edition (2017) removed microscopic extrathyroidal extension (mETE) from T-staging, reserving T3b for gross strap-muscle invasion and T4a/T4b for deeper structures.5 The 2025 ATA guidelines retained the AJCC 8th edition approach of excluding mETE from T-staging while incorporating mETE into postoperative recurrence-risk stratification, emphasizing individualized management rather than automatic treatment escalation.6 The new four-tier framework reduces the weight assigned to isolated mETE at the population level while leaving open the possibility that its association with recurrence varies by clinical context, including nodal status.

Despite this consensus, published evidence is strikingly heterogeneous. A supplementary literature review (819 studies screened, 80 extracted) suggests that conflicting findings are driven by tumor size, patient age, treatment intensity, and—critically—endpoint selection. Large population-based studies (Bortz et al., N = 177,497; Liu et al., N = 107,114) consistently report mETE-associated survival decrements using endpoints independent of staging classification.7,8 Conversely, studies using staging-derived proxies or examining selected low-risk populations find no independent effect.9,10 The seed papers illustrate this tension: Parvathareddy et al. (2021; N = 1,430) found mETE independently predicted recurrence (HR 1.75) on a structural endpoint,11 whereas Patti et al. (2023; N = 100) reported that modified ATA risk downstaging mETE improved specificity on a staging-derived proxy.12

We analyzed 3,278 PTC patients with validated three-tier ETE classification using both a composite recurrence risk band and a structural disease endpoint. Propensity score matching isolated the mETE effect on structural disease; formal interaction tests identified potential effect modifiers. CT imaging timing was characterized to determine the fraction of structural endpoint events attributable to post-operative disease versus peri-operative staging workup. We hypothesized that mETE carries context-dependent prognostic significance that is masked by composite proxies but detectable on structural disease—particularly in node-negative patients and larger tumors.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a single academic tertiary center. Patient data were drawn from a structured institutional thyroid cancer research database containing 11,673 patients. The analytic code and derived views used to build the study cohort are described in the Supplement and publicly archived (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18945510). To characterize CT imaging timing, we linked all CT date entries in the institutional database to each patient’s first surgery date, achieving 100% date coverage after recovering 50 previously missing dates from free-text radiology reports using natural language processing. The study was approved by institutional review board approval; informed consent was waived (see Ethical Approval).

Primary analysis outcome: composite recurrence risk band. This was a three-tier proxy outcome (low, intermediate, or high risk) derived from AJCC 8th edition stage, gross ETE status, and peak thyroglobulin level. An important caveat: because gross ETE is built directly into the high-risk definition, the gross ETE regression coefficient is circular and cannot be interpreted. The mETE coefficient—our variable of interest—is not part of the derivation and can be estimated, though its interpretation is still shaped by the staging- and thyroglobulin-derived nature of the outcome.

Secondary analysis outcome: structural disease endpoint. We defined structural disease as cross-sectional imaging evidence of pathologic lymphadenopathy on CT or MRI, or reoperation. Neck ultrasound was not included in the endpoint definition. Because this definition may capture persistent disease (never fully cleared after initial surgery) as well as true recurrence, we refer to it as a structural disease endpoint throughout. A total of 504 of 3,278 patients (15.4%) met this endpoint. Disease-free survival (DFS) was measured from the surgery date to the last thyroglobulin measurement, with censoring based on structural endpoint status.

To assess potential peri-operative ascertainment bias, we linked 3,018 CT examination rows among 650 PTC patients to each patient’s first surgery date, classifying each by timing: preoperative, perioperative (≤30 days post-surgery), postoperative 30 days–1 year, or postoperative >1 year. Among these, 331 patients had ≥1 pathologic-lymphadenopathy-flagged examination, accounting for 1,245 flagged examination rows.

Primary analysis. We used ordinal logistic regression (a proportional odds model, which compares ordered risk categories) to model the composite risk band, adjusting for age, sex, tumor size, and lymph node ratio. The proportional odds assumption—that the effect of each predictor is consistent across risk-band thresholds—was tested and confirmed for mETE (coefficient difference across cut-points: 0.23). The gross ETE variable violated this assumption (difference: 8.12), consistent with its circularity in the outcome. We assessed model discrimination using apparent and five-fold cross-validated AUC. Sensitivity analyses included multiple imputation (m = 20), age-stratified models (≥55 vs. <55), restriction to tumors ≤4 cm, and a classic-variant subgroup.

Structural disease analysis. To isolate the mETE effect on structural disease, we used propensity score matching (PSM)—a technique that pairs mETE and no-ETE patients who are otherwise similar on measured covariates. Gross ETE patients were excluded. Propensity scores were estimated via logistic regression on age, sex, tumor size, and N1 status (any positive lymph node). We used nearest-neighbor matching with a caliper of 0.05. The matched effect was estimated as an odds ratio using Fisher’s exact test. Covariate balance was assessed with standardized mean differences (SMD; target <0.10). Matched DFS was compared using Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank testing.

CT imaging timing analysis. For each CT-detected pathologic lymphadenopathy event among the 331 flagged patients (1,245 events), we calculated the number of days from the index surgery and classified it into mutually exclusive timing categories: preoperative, perioperative (≤30 days post-surgery), postoperative 31–365 days, and postoperative >365 days. The rationale: preoperative and perioperative CT events likely reflect staging workup rather than true recurrence. If this misclassification is non-differential by ETE status—meaning it affects mETE and no-ETE patients equally—it would bias the estimated association toward the null. However, we cannot exclude differential postoperative imaging intensity once clinicians know the mETE finding.

All interaction terms and stratified models were pre-specified in the analysis plan (archived repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18945510).

The central finding is that mETE showed differing associations depending on endpoint within the same cohort: OR 0.60 (inverse) on a composite proxy versus OR 1.43 (adverse, p = 0.030) on propensity-matched structural disease. The composite proxy incorporates AJCC 8th staging, which excludes mETE from T-classification; regressing mETE on an outcome already purged of mETE information produces a null or inverse coefficient by construction. The structural endpoint is classification-independent and captures actual disease behavior. CT imaging timing analysis provides additional context: 40.8% of events were preoperative and 5.9% perioperative (together 46.7%, likely staging workup), while 53.3% occurred later, though differential surveillance intensity cannot be excluded. This endpoint dependency likely explains much of the published heterogeneity: studies using staging-derived proxies tend to find mETE non-prognostic, whereas studies using structural disease endpoints tend to find it prognostic.

The mETE × nodal-status interaction is hypothesis-generating and suggests that any adverse association may be concentrated in node-negative disease, where mETE may be the sole indicator of aggressive biology beyond tumor size. In node-positive patients, mETE appears informationally redundant. The tumor-size dose-response (OR 1.32–1.57) further supports context dependence, though the formal interaction was non-significant (p = 0.412). The age-dependent attenuation (OR 0.44 in age <55 vs. 0.87 in ≥55) is consistent with Tran et al.’s finding of mETE predicting reduced DFS (HR 2.8) specifically in patients ≥55.18

Our findings are concordant with the 2025 ATA guidelines.6 The framework appropriately avoids using mETE alone for population-level stage assignment while allowing individualized surveillance. The ΔAUC of 0.025 confirms negligible discriminative contribution at the population level. The 71.5% T-stage downstaging among mETE patients confirms the magnitude of AJCC 8th edition stage migration; under 7th edition rules, over 1,200 patients would have been classified as T3. Our mETE × nodal interaction (p = 0.006) suggests node-negative patients with tumors >2 cm may represent a subgroup where mETE carries modest additional information for surveillance planning.

Several limitations merit discussion. First, the primary outcome was a composite proxy derived from AJCC stage, gross ETE status, and peak thyroglobulin; the proxy analysis should be interpreted as classification-dependent. Because gross ETE is embedded in the high-risk definition, the gross ETE coefficient is circular, although this does not affect the mETE estimate. Second, covariate adjustment was limited: the lymph node ratio behaved as a binary variable (99.0% of values 0 or 1), M-stage was meaningful for only 241/3,278 patients (7.4%; sensitivity analysis confirmed no material change), and treatment confounding (surgery extent, neck dissection, RAI dose, TSH suppression) was not modeled. Third, thyroglobulin follow-up was sparse (mETE median 0.0 years), constraining longitudinal analyses and the DFS censoring definition.

Fourth, the structural endpoint is vulnerable to peri-operative imaging contamination: of 1,245 CT-detected pathologic lymphadenopathy events, 508 (40.8%) were preoperative and 73 (5.9%) were perioperative. For pathologists, explicit mETE documentation remains essential. For surgeons and endocrinologists, incidental mETE alone should not automatically trigger completion thyroidectomy or RAI; management should be individualized considering tumor size, nodal status, and postoperative response. Node-negative patients with mETE in tumors >2 cm may warrant closer surveillance, pending external validation. For researchers, endpoint selection critically determines whether mETE appears prognostic; future studies should prefer structural disease endpoints.

In 3,278 PTC patients, microscopic extrathyroidal extension showed differing associations depending on endpoint: inversely associated on a composite staging-derived proxy (OR 0.60, p < 0.001) but associated with modestly higher structural disease in propensity-matched analysis (OR 1.43, p = 0.030). A significant mETE × nodal-status interaction (p = 0.006) suggests that this association was concentrated in node-negative patients, with a dose-response trend across tumor sizes (OR 1.32–1.57).

Two nodal-status variables appeared in different analytic contexts. The lymph node ratio (histology_1_ln_ratio), defined as the proportion of examined nodes that were positive, was used as a covariate in ordinal logistic regression; in practice, 99.0% of values in the analytic cohort were 0 or 1, so it functioned as a binary indicator and is labeled accordingly in Table 2. Separately, the N1 status variable (ct_pathologic_ln_flag), indicating any pathologic node-positive disease, was used in propensity score matching to balance nodal burden between mETE and no-ETE groups. Both variables capture nodal involvement but at different levels of granularity; their roles are analytically distinct and are not interchangeable in the models reported.

A database-level linkage joined all CT examination date fields to each patient’s first surgery date, achieving 100% date coverage after NLP recovery of 50 previously missing dates. Within the PTC analytic cohort, this linkage produced ptc_ct_imaging_events (3,018 rows, 650 PTC patients). Among these, 331 patients had ≥1 row with ct_pathologic_ln_flag = True, yielding 1,245 flagged examination rows. Timing categories for these 1,245 events: 508 preoperative, 73 perioperative (≤30 days post-surgery), 174 postoperative 31–364 days, and 490 postoperative ≥365 days.

> We studied **3,278** patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) from a curated institutional cohort; a classic-variant subset comprised **596** patients. Extrathyroidal extension was classified as absent, microscopic (mETE), or gross. The primary analysis modeled ATA recurrence risk category (ordinal) under AJCC 8th staging. In matched analysis, structural burden was more frequent with mETE (absolute difference **3.9** percentage points; odds ratio **1.43**, Fisher **p = 0.03**), with **imperfect post-match balance for nodal disease** (standardized mean difference **−0.58** for N1). On formal interaction testing, **mETE×age was not significant** (**p = 0.26**), while **mETE×N1 was significant** (**p = 0.006**). > **ETE classification.** Gross ETE corresponded to `tumor_1_gross_ete` = 1. Any pathologic extrathyroidal extension without gross criteria was classified as microscopic ETE (`tumor_1_extrathyroidal_ext` true and not gross). Absence of extension was classified as no ETE.

> **Structural endpoint.** For secondary analyses, `structural_recurrence` was 1 if either: (i) the imaging correlation layer indicated **pathologic lymphadenopathy on CT or MRI** (`ct_pathologic_ln_flag` or `mri_pathologic_ln_flag`), or (ii) **more than one distinct surgery date** appeared in the pathology-linked surgery table (`reoperation_proxy`).

> **Nodal variables.** **N1 status** (`n_positive_flag`: `n_stage_ajcc8` beginning with “N1”) was used in propensity matching and structural logistic models. **Lymph node ratio** (`ln_ratio`) was used in **ordinal** models as pre-specified; in our data `ln_examined` was highly discrete (often binary), so **`ln_ratio` behaved as a quasi-binary positivity burden** with substantial missingness—results are presented alongside **N1** (Table 1).

> Baseline **N1** prevalence differed across ETE groups (expanded cohort: **56.9%** no ETE, **67.2%** mETE, **74.7%** gross ETE; *P* < 0.001). ### 4.5 Discussion — nodal effect modification vs age attenuation (paragraph)

> We separated **three distinct issues**: (i) **baseline** higher nodal prevalence in mETE relative to no ETE in expanded cohort Tabulations; (ii) **formal interaction** on the structural logistic scale, which was **significant for N1** but **not for age**; and (iii) **descriptive attenuation** of the microscopic ETE association with **composite** risk category among older adults in ordinal sensitivity analyses—this pattern should **not** be labeled as effect modification without a significant product term. Propensity matching did **not** achieve satisfactory **nodal balance** (SMD **−0.58** for N1 despite inclusion in the propensity model), so structural comparisons should be framed as **hypothesis-generating** and potentially confounded by residual lymphatic burden.

> Microscopic ETE mapped to **substantially higher pathologic N1 rates** than no ETE in both classic and all-PTC cohorts (classic: **68.3%** vs **44.3%**; expanded: **67.2%** vs **56.9%**), indicating that **mETE in this database identifies patients with heavier baseline nodal involvement** independent of its association with composite recurrence-risk category on multivariable ordinal analysis.

> We prespecified two complementary estimands. **First**, an **ordinal logistic model** for institutionally derived **recurrence risk category** adjusted for age, sex, size, and **lymph node ratio**, acknowledging that **gross ETE largely determines the highest category** (so gross ETE coefficients are not interpreted causally) and that **node ratio is sparse/quasi-binary**. **Second**, a **binary structural burden endpoint** (imaging pathologic nodes **or** reoperation) with **1:1 propensity matching** of mETE to no ETE on age, sex, size, and **N1**, reporting Fisher and standardized differences; we highlight **worsened N1 balance post-match** and a **significant mETE×N1 interaction** but **no mETE×age interaction**. **CT results** are purely descriptive and use **examination-level** extracts with explicit pre- versus post-surgical timing relative to index surgery.

# Proposal 2: AJCC 8th Edition Staging and Microscopic vs Gross ETE

This analysis examines the prognostic significance of microscopic extrathyroidal extension (mETE) versus gross ETE in a cohort of 596 classic papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) patients staged under the AJCC 8th edition. Among our cohort, 185 (31.0%) had no ETE, 249 (41.8%) had microscopic ETE, and 162 (27.2%) had gross ETE. Stage migration analysis reveals that 172 patients with mETE experienced T-stage downstaging under AJCC 8th edition rules (69.4% of mETE cases). Overall, 348 patients (58.7%) were downstaged from AJCC 7th to 8th edition. Ordinal logistic regression demonstrates that gross ETE, but not microscopic ETE alone, independently predicts higher recurrence risk after adjustment for age, sex, tumor size, and lymph node ratio—supporting the AJCC 8th edition decision to exclude mETE from T-staging. Adding microscopic ETE to predictive models produces minimal improvement in AUC for high recurrence risk prediction (ΔAUC = 0.014).

This study leverages a well-curated institutional database of 596 classic PTC patients with structured, pathologist-verified ETE classification to evaluate the impact of the AJCC 8th edition's decision to remove microscopic ETE from T-staging. Our data demonstrate three key findings: (1) microscopic ETE is common (41.8% of PTC cases) and its removal from staging criteria results in substantial downstaging (69% T-stage, 67% overall stage migration); (2) gross ETE, but not microscopic ETE, independently predicts higher recurrence risk on multivariable ordinal logistic regression; and (3) adding microscopic ETE to existing prognostic models yields negligible improvement in discrimination (ΔAUC = 0.014). These findings broadly support the AJCC 8th edition reclassification and are consistent with the conclusions of Kim et al. (2023, J Endocrinol Invest, N=100) and Yin et al. (2021, Frontiers in Oncology, N=1,430), while extending those findings in a larger, single-institution cohort with granular ETE subtyping and thyroglobulin trajectory data.

Several limitations warrant discussion. First, the recurrence risk band is a composite proxy derived from AJCC stage, gross ETE status, and peak thyroglobulin rather than a directly observed recurrence event; true time-to-recurrence data would strengthen the survival analysis. Second, inter-observer variability in distinguishing microscopic from gross ETE at the time of pathologic examination may introduce misclassification. Third, the cohort is limited to classic-variant PTC and may not generalize to aggressive histologic subtypes (tall cell, hobnail, columnar cell). Fourth, molecular markers (BRAF V600E, TERT promoter) were not consistently available for integration. Clinically, these findings have direct implications: (1) surgeons and pathologists should continue to report ETE subtype (microscopic vs. gross) to enable risk stratification refinement; (2) microscopic ETE alone should not trigger escalation of treatment intensity (e.g., completion thyroidectomy, RAI dose escalation); and (3) the AJCC 8th edition staging system appropriately captures the prognostic heterogeneity of ETE, supporting its adoption without modification for mETE.

**1. Pathology Reporting: Distinguish Microscopic from Gross ETE.** Our cohort demonstrates that microscopic ETE accounts for 41.8% of classic PTC cases, making it the most common ETE subtype. Despite its prevalence, mETE was consistently associated with lower odds of higher recurrence risk classification across all analytic specifications (pooled OR range 0.30–0.60, all p < 0.001). The 2025 ATA guidelines reaffirm that mETE should not be incorporated into T-staging but emphasize continued documentation to support individualized risk assessment. Pathology reports should explicitly state the ETE subtype—microscopic only, gross with strap muscle involvement (T3b), or gross beyond strap muscles (T4a)—to enable downstream clinical decision-making.

Third, standardization of mETE histopathologic reporting criteria across institutions will reduce inter-observer variability and improve external validity of future studies.
